procedural_history.originating_court: Special Judge (PC-ACT), Rouse Avenue Court Complex, New Delhi
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 18.07.2023 passed by the High Court of Delhi at New Delhi in Bail Application No. 152 of 2023.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant filed a bail application (No. 152 of 2023) before the High Court of Delhi, which was rejected vide order dated 18.07.2023.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellant-accused, being aggrieved by the High Court's order dated 18.07.2023, preferred an appeal to the Supreme Court (Criminal Appeal No. 3593 of 2023).

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in dismissing the bail application of the appellant in a case concerning the offence of money laundering under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, which arose from an FIR for offences under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 and the Indian Penal Code.

facts: The appellant was arrested in a money laundering case under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA).
The PMLA case arose from a predicate offence FIR registered under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, and various sections of the Indian Penal Code.
The appellant's bail applications were previously dismissed by the Special Judge and then by the High Court.
The appellant argued that he should be granted bail because the investigation against him was complete, the trial was likely to take a long time, and other co-accused had been granted bail.
law: Section 45 of the PMLA imposes two mandatory conditions for granting bail: the court must have reasonable grounds to believe that the accused is (1) not guilty of the offence and (2) not likely to commit any offence while on bail.
The burden of proof to satisfy these conditions lies on the accused.
Section 71 of the PMLA gives the Act an overriding effect, meaning the stringent conditions of Section 45 must be complied with even for bail applications under the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC).
Economic offences are considered a grave class of crime that must be viewed seriously, as they affect the financial health of the country.
application: The Court held that the appellant had failed to overcome the mandatory threshold stipulations of Section 45 of the PMLA.
Specifically, the appellant did not prima facie prove that he was not guilty of the alleged offence of money laundering.
The Court noted that, contrary to the appellant's claims, there was sufficient material on record presented by the prosecution showing the appellant's "thick involvement" in the crime.

The Court rejected the appellant's arguments regarding the length of the trial and parity with other co-accused, stating that the failure to meet the conditions of Section 45 was the primary reason for denial of bail.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appeal and upheld the High Court's decision to dismiss the bail application. The Court found that the appellant failed to satisfy the mandatory twin conditions for bail under Section 45 of the PMLA, as he could not discharge the burden of proving, on a prima facie basis, that he was not guilty of the offence of money laundering.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in dismissing the bail application of the appellant in a case concerning the offence of money laundering under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, which arose from an FIR for offences under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 and the Indian Penal Code.
appellant_arguments: The allegations and the roles attributed to the appellant in the commission of the alleged offences are baseless.
The appellant was not named as an accused in the first complaint or the second and third supplementary complaints, despite being summoned for investigation multiple times before they were filed.
The appellant was only arraigned as an accused in the fourth supplementary complaint after being arrested on 22.06.2022, suggesting the case against him is an afterthought.
respondent_arguments: Statements of witnesses/accused recorded under Section 50 of the PMLA are admissible in evidence and make out a formidable case about the appellant's involvement in a serious offence of money laundering.

Apart from witness statements, there is sufficient documentary material collected that prima facie shows the appellant was knowingly a party to and actually involved in the process and activities connected with the proceeds of crime.
The evidence demonstrates how the appellant was involved in projecting/claiming such proceeds of crime as untainted.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The principle of parity is based on the guarantee of positive equality before the law under Article 14 of the Constitution; however, if an illegality or irregularity has been committed in favor of an individual, others cannot invoke the jurisdiction of a higher court to repeat or multiply that same illegality.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court held that economic offences constitute a distinct category of crime that must be approached differently in matters of bail. Given their deep-rooted conspiracies, the significant loss of public funds involved, and their detrimental effect on the national economy, they are considered grave offences. Therefore, when considering a bail application for such crimes, a court must conduct a prima facie evaluation of the evidence and the nature of the accusations, keeping in mind the severity of the potential punishment and the larger public interest.
legal_tests_applied: The twin conditions for bail under Section 45(1) of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, which require that: (i) the Public Prosecutor has been given an opportunity to oppose the application for such release; and (ii) where the Public Prosecutor opposes the application, the court is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for believing that he is not guilty of such offence and that he is not likely to commit any offence while on bail.
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the appellant's submission that bail cannot be denied merely because the crime is an economic offence, stating, 'In our opinion, there is hardly any merit in the said submission of Mr. Luthra.'

The court implicitly rejected the argument for bail based on parity (that other allegedly involved persons have not been arrested) by endorsing the principle that 'Article 14 is not meant to perpetuate the illegality or irregularity. If there has been a benefit or advantage conferred on one or a set of people by any authority or by the court, without legal basis or justification, other persons could not claim as a matter of right the benefit on the basis of such wrong decision.'
why_respondent_won: The court accepted the respondent's argument that the stringent twin conditions for bail contained in Section 45(1) of the PMLA would apply to the appellant due to the seriousness of the offence.

The court's reasoning aligned with the respondent's position by emphasizing that economic offences must be viewed seriously, as they affect the economy of the country as a whole and pose a threat to its financial health.
policy_considerations: Economic offences constitute a class apart and need to be visited with a different approach in the matter of bail.

Such offences having deep-rooted conspiracies and involving huge loss of public funds need to be viewed seriously and considered as grave offences affecting the economy of the country as a whole and thereby posing serious threat to the financial health of the country.

The entire community is aggrieved if the economic offenders who ruin the economy of the State are not brought to books. An economic offence is committed with cool calculation and deliberate design with an eye on personal profit regardless of the consequence to the community.
A disregard for the interest of the community can be manifested only at the cost of forfeiting the trust and faith of the community in the system to administer justice in an even-handed manner.
